Section 1: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) - Job Search and Application Optimizer based on AI¶

Job Description Dataset¶

This notebook presents an exploratory data analysis of a job listings dataset. The goal is to understand the structure, identify data quality issues, and extract meaningful insights to support further modeling.

5 rows × 23 columns

This dataset provides a comprehensive collection of synthetic job postings to facilitate research and analysis in the field of job market trends, natural language processing (NLP), and machine learning. Created for educational and research purposes, this dataset offers a diverse set of job listings across various industries and job types.

Descriptions for each of the columns in the dataset:

  • Job Id: A unique identifier for each job posting.
  • Experience: The required or preferred years of experience for the job.
  • Qualifications: The educational qualifications needed for the job.
  • Salary Range: The range of salaries or compensation offered for the position.
  • Location: The city or area where the job is located.
  • Country: The country where the job is located.
  • Latitude: The latitude coordinate of the job location.
  • Longitude: The longitude coordinate of the job location.
  • Work Type: The type of employment (e.g., full-time, part-time, contract).
  • Company Size: The approximate size or scale of the hiring company.
  • Job Posting Date: The date when the job posting was made public.
  • Preference: Special preferences or requirements for applicants (e.g., Only Male or Only Female, or Both)
  • Contact Person: The name of the contact person or recruiter for the job.
  • Contact: Contact information for job inquiries.
  • Job Title: The job title or position being advertised.
  • Role: The role or category of the job (e.g., software developer, marketing manager).
  • Job Portal: The platform or website where the job was posted.
  • Job Description: A detailed description of the job responsibilities and requirements.
  • Benefits: Information about benefits offered with the job (e.g., health insurance, retirement plans).
  • Skills: The skills or qualifications required for the job.
  • Responsibilities: Specific responsibilities and duties associated with the job.
  • Company Name: The name of the hiring company.
  • Company Profile: A brief overview of the company's background and mission.

The dataset shows a high level of completeness across its attributes, as almost all columns contain the full set of non-null records. Out of the 23 available columns and a total of 1,615,940 entries, only the Company Profile column contains missing values, with 1,610,462 non-null records. This minimal amount of missing data is likely due to the fact that the dataset is synthetic, meaning it was artificially generated and designed to maintain a high level of consistency and completeness across most variables.

The statistical analysis shows that the dataset contains a large variety of job-related information with high diversity across most categorical variables.

For the numerical variable Company Size, the average company size is approximately 73,705 employees, with a standard deviation of 35,299, indicating a wide variation in company sizes. The smallest company in the dataset has around 12,646 employees, while the largest reaches 134,834 employees. The median value (73,633) is very close to the mean, suggesting a relatively balanced distribution.

Regarding categorical variables, the dataset contains 48 different experience categories, with “5 to 8 Years” being the most frequent. There are 10 qualification categories, where BBA appears most commonly. Salary ranges are highly diverse, with 561 unique salary intervals, although “$59K-$88K” is the most repeated range.

The dataset also demonstrates broad geographic coverage, including 214 unique locations and 216 countries, with Seoul and Malta appearing most frequently. For employment conditions, Part-Time positions are the most common work type, while Male is the most frequent preference category.

Job-related fields such as Job Title, Role, Job Description, Skills, and Responsibilities show a high diversity of professional profiles, although UX/UI Designer and Interaction Designer related entries appear most often. Similarly, FlexJobs is the most represented job portal in the dataset.

Finally, company-related information is also diverse, with 888 unique companies and 884 different company profiles. The most frequent company is DTE Energy, while the most common company profile corresponds to an automotive sector organization. Overall, these statistics suggest that the synthetic dataset was designed to simulate a broad and diverse job market environment.

In [9]:
df["desc_length"] = df["Job Description"].str.len()
df["skills_length"] = df["skills"].str.len()
df["resp_length"] = df["Responsibilities"].str.len()
df["skills_count"] = df["skills"].apply(lambda x: len(x.split(",")))

Feature extraction was applied to create new numerical variables from the text columns. The variables desc_length, skills_length, and resp_length measure the length of the job description, skills, and responsibilities text.

Additionally, skills_count counts how many skills are listed in each job posting by separating the skills using commas. These new features help transform textual information into measurable data for analysis and modeling.

The skewness analysis shows how the data is distributed for each numerical variable:

  • Company Size (0.002) → Almost perfectly symmetric, meaning company sizes are evenly distributed around the mean.
  • desc_length (1.007) → Positively skewed, indicating that most job descriptions are shorter, while a smaller number contain very long descriptions.
  • skills_length (0.770) → Moderately positively skewed, showing that most skill descriptions have medium length, but some are significantly longer.
  • resp_length (-0.017) → Nearly symmetric, meaning responsibility descriptions are distributed evenly without strong skewness.
  • skills_count (2.691) → Highly positively skewed, indicating that most job postings list a small number of skills, while a few postings contain a very large number of skills.

Salary Cleaning¶

Salary ranges are transformed into numerical values for analysis.

In [19]:
def clean_salary(s):
    if pd.isna(s):
        return np.nan
    s = s.replace("$", "").replace("K", "000").replace("−", "-")
    parts = s.split("-")
    return (int(parts[0]) + int(parts[1])) / 2

df["Salary"] = df["Salary Range"].apply(clean_salary)

def extract_experience(exp):
    exp = exp.replace("Years", "").strip()
    parts = exp.split("to")
    return (int(parts[0]) + int(parts[1])) / 2

df["Experience_num"] = df["Experience"].apply(extract_experience)

Outlier Detection¶

In [36]:
q1 = df["Salary"].quantile(0.25)
q3 = df["Salary"].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1

outliers = df[(df["Salary"] < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (df["Salary"] > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)]
len(outliers)
Out[36]:
0
In [37]:
upper_limit = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
lower_limit = q1 - 1.5 * iqr

df["Salary_capped"] = df["Salary"].clip(lower_limit, upper_limit)

The function to measure the quality of a split. Supported criteria

max_features max_features: {"sqrt", "log2", None}, int or float, default=1.0

The number of features to consider when looking for the best split:

- If int, then consider `max_features` features at each split.
- If float, then `max_features` is a fraction and
`max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))` features are considered at each

- If "sqrt", then `max_features=sqrt(n_features)`.
- If "log2", then `max_features=log2(n_features)`.

Note: the search for a split does not stop until at least one
valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to

max_leaf_nodes max_leaf_nodes: int, default=None

Grow trees with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
If None then unlimited number of leaf nodes. 		None
min_impurity_decrease min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
- N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

EDA Findings and Conclusions¶

Missing Values¶

The dataset contains very few missing values. Only the Company Profile column presents missing entries, with 5,478 null values, representing approximately 0.34% of the dataset. All other variables are complete.

No strong missing-value patterns were identified, suggesting that the dataset is generally well-structured and suitable for analysis without aggressive imputation strategies.

Summary Statistics¶

The dataset contains 1,615,940 job postings and 23 variables.

Key numerical observations:

  • Company Size has a mean of approximately 73,704 employees.
  • Latitude values range from -40.90 to 71.70.
  • Longitude values range from -175.20 to 178.06.
  • Salary ranges were transformed into numerical salary estimates for analysis.

Key categorical observations:

  • Qualifications contains 10 categories.
  • Work Type contains 5 categories.
  • Country contains 216 unique values.
  • Company contains 888 unique values.

The dataset combines structured numerical data with high-dimensional textual information.

Outlier Analysis¶

Outlier detection was performed using the IQR method on the salary variable.

No significant salary outliers were identified under the standard 1.5 × IQR rule. However, salary distributions still exhibit moderate variability, suggesting that capped or transformed versions may still improve modeling stability.

Cardinality of Categorical Variables¶

Several categorical variables exhibit high cardinality:

  • Contact: 1,615,933 unique values
  • Contact Person: 367,128 unique values
  • Company: 888 unique values
  • Role: 376 unique values
  • Job Description: 376 unique values

These variables may negatively affect machine learning models if encoded directly. Frequency encoding or feature extraction techniques are more appropriate for these cases.

Skewed Distributions and Transformations¶

The salary distribution showed moderate skewness. To reduce skewness and stabilize variance, a logarithmic transformation (log1p) was applied to the salary variable.

Text-based features such as job description length and skills length also exhibited non-normal distributions.

Temporal Trends¶

The dataset includes a temporal variable: Job Posting Date.

After converting the column to datetime format, yearly posting trends were analyzed. The dataset mainly contains job postings from 2022 and 2023, with relatively stable posting activity over time.

No major seasonal fluctuations were observed at the yearly aggregation level.

Correlation Analysis¶

Correlation analysis revealed generally weak to moderate relationships between numerical features and salary.

The most relevant engineered features included:

  • Experience_num
  • Company Size
  • skills_count
  • desc_length

Feature relevance analysis using a Random Forest model confirmed that experience-related and text-derived variables contributed more strongly to salary prediction than geographic variables.

Bivariate Analysis¶

Several bivariate analyses were performed:

  • Salary distribution by Work Type
  • Salary distribution by Experience
  • Relationship between experience and salary using scatterplots and regression plots

Results suggest that higher experience levels tend to correspond to higher salary ranges, although variability remains high across categories.

Different work types also show distinct salary distributions.

Image Normalization¶

This dataset does not contain image data; therefore, image normalization was not required.

Class Imbalance¶

The Work Type variable shows moderate class imbalance.

Some categories, such as Part-Time, appear significantly more frequently than others. This imbalance should be considered during future modeling stages, especially for classification tasks.

General Conclusions¶

  • The dataset is large, diverse, and mostly clean.
  • Textual variables represent an important source of information.
  • High-cardinality categorical variables require preprocessing strategies.
  • Salary and experience exhibit meaningful relationships.
  • Feature engineering significantly improves feature relevance analysis.
  • The dataset is suitable for predictive modeling and NLP applications.
  • The exploratory analysis suggests that the dataset can be extended with synthetic ranking labels associated with specific professional roles, such as Software Engineer, Data Scientist, or Product Manager.
  • By incorporating ranking scores for each job posting, the dataset can be transformed into a supervised learning problem where the model learns to predict the relevance or quality ranking of a job opportunity given its role, skills, experience requirements, and description.
  • This preprocessing and feature engineering pipeline provides a strong foundation for building a job recommendation or ranking system.

Section 2: Feature Engineering and Data Preparation for Machine Learning¶

In this section, we transform the raw job postings dataset into a structured dataset suitable for machine learning.

We perform feature extraction, encoding, scaling preparation, feature selection, and transformations to reduce skewness and improve model readiness.

This stage prepares the dataset for a future supervised learning system that will predict job compatibility scores.

2. Outlier Detection using IQR¶

We detect outliers in numerical variables using the Interquartile Range (IQR) method.

In [52]:
numeric_cols = ["Company Size", "desc_length", "skills_length", "resp_length", "skills_count"]

outlier_summary = {}

for col in numeric_cols:
    Q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1

    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

    outliers = df[(df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)]
    outlier_summary[col] = len(outliers)

outlier_summary

The Experience field was decomposed into minimum, maximum, and average values to convert a textual range into structured numerical features. This allows the model to capture both variability and central tendency of required experience.

In [60]:
def extract_experience_ranges(exp):
    exp = exp.replace("Years", "").strip()

    parts = exp.split("to")

    exp_min = int(parts[0].strip())
    exp_max = int(parts[1].strip())

    exp_avg = (exp_min + exp_max) / 2

    return pd.Series([exp_min, exp_max, exp_avg])

df[["Experience_min", "Experience_max", "Experience_avg"]] = (
    df["Experience"].apply(extract_experience_ranges)
)
In [61]:
def parse_company_profile(profile):
    try:
        data = json.loads(profile)

        sector = data.get("Sector", np.nan)
        industry = data.get("Industry", np.nan)
        state = data.get("State", np.nan)

        has_ticker = 0 if data.get("Ticker", "") == "" else 1
        has_website = 0 if data.get("Website", "") == "" else 1

        return pd.Series([
            sector,
            industry,
            state,
            has_ticker,
            has_website
        ])

    except:
        return pd.Series([np.nan]*5)

df[[
    "Company_Sector",
    "Company_Industry",
    "Company_State",
    "Has_Ticker",
    "Has_Website"
]] = df["Company Profile"].apply(parse_company_profile)

Summary for the section #2 (CRISP-ML Phase)¶

During the data preparation phase, the original job postings dataset was transformed into a structured, enriched, and machine learning–ready dataset. The objective of this stage was to convert raw heterogeneous data (text, categorical, numerical, and semi-structured fields) into meaningful features suitable for predictive modeling and natural language processing tasks.

Feature Engineering and Transformations¶

Several feature engineering techniques were applied to improve the dataset’s representational power and predictive capacity:

  • Text-based feature extraction was performed on unstructured fields such as Job Description, Skills, Responsibilities, and Benefits. These features include:

    • Character-based length metrics (desc_length, skills_length, resp_length)
    • Word-level complexity metrics (job_desc_word_count, skills_word_count, resp_word_count)
    • Skill and benefit aggregation metrics (skills_count, benefits_count)

  • Experience transformation was applied to convert the original categorical range into numerical variables:

    • Experience_min
    • Experience_max
    • Experience_avg This decomposition allows models to capture nonlinear effects of experience more effectively than ordinal encoding.

  • Salary preprocessing included:

    • Conversion from string ranges into numerical values (Salary)
    • Log transformation (Salary_log) to reduce skewness and stabilize variance

  • Company-level feature enrichment:

    • Frequency encoding (Company_freq) was used to reduce high cardinality effects

    • Structured parsing of Company Profile extracted:

      • Sector
      • Industry
      • State
      • Binary indicators: Has_Ticker, Has_Website

These transformations improve feature interpretability while reducing noise and dimensionality issues.

Data Quality and Preparation¶

  • Missing values were minimal (0.34% in Company Profile) and did not require aggressive imputation strategies.
  • High-cardinality categorical variables were identified and handled using appropriate encoding strategies (frequency encoding or preservation for NLP usage).
  • Salary outliers were analyzed using the IQR method, with no extreme outliers detected under the standard threshold.
  • All raw text fields were preserved to enable future NLP-based embedding and semantic similarity models.

Scaling, Transformation, and Normalization¶

To ensure compatibility with machine learning algorithms sensitive to feature magnitude:

  • Log transformation was applied to salary to reduce skewness and improve distribution symmetry.
  • Standardization (StandardScaler) was applied to selected numerical features to ensure comparable scale across variables.
  • Skewness analysis guided transformation decisions, particularly for text-derived features such as skills_count and desc_length, which showed moderate to high positive skew.

These steps improve model convergence stability and prevent dominance of high-scale variables.

Feature Selection and Extraction¶

Feature selection was performed using a combination of:

  • Random Forest feature importance
  • Correlation analysis with the target variable (Salary)
  • Variance and distribution inspection

The most relevant features identified were:

  • Company Size
  • Company_freq
  • Experience_num
  • desc_length
  • skills_length
  • resp_length

Less informative variables such as skills_count showed lower predictive contribution and were deprioritized.

This process reduced model complexity while maintaining predictive power and interpretability.

Final Dataset Structure¶

The resulting dataset integrates three complementary types of features:

  1. Structured numerical and categorical variables for classical machine learning models
  2. Engineered text-derived features capturing job complexity and content richness
  3. Raw text fields preserved for NLP-based approaches such as embeddings and semantic search

This hybrid structure ensures compatibility with both traditional ML pipelines and modern NLP-driven recommender systems.

Next Steps: Synthetic Label Generation¶

Since the dataset does not contain explicit target labels for job relevance or recommendation quality, a synthetic labeling strategy will be introduced to enable supervised learning.

Two target variables will be created:

  • Job_Family: A categorical label representing the professional domain of each job (e.g., Software Engineering, Data Science, Marketing, Healthcare). This will be generated using rule-based classification based on keywords, job roles, and skill mappings.

  • Compatibility_Score (1–5): A synthetic ranking variable representing how well a job matches an ideal candidate profile. It will be constructed using:

    • Skill overlap between job postings and predefined profiles
    • Experience level alignment
    • Semantic similarity (future extension using embedding-based methods)

These labels will transform the dataset into a supervised learning problem suitable for job ranking and recommendation systems.

CRISP-ML Context¶

This phase completes the data preparation stage of CRISP-ML by delivering a clean, structured, and feature-rich dataset ready for modeling.

Key achievements include:

  • Feature engineering from raw text and structured data
  • Normalization and transformation for statistical stability
  • Feature selection to reduce complexity and improve interpretability
  • Preservation of raw text for NLP extensions

The next phase will focus on synthetic labeling and model development for job classification and recommendation.

Section 3: Knowledge Distillation & Synthetic Label Generation for Job Alignment Scoring¶

The goal of this section is to train a supervised regression model capable of predicting how aligned a given job posting is to a user's desired role (the "comparator"), outputting a continuous score from 0.0 (completely unrelated) to 5.0 (perfect match). This model serves as the scoring engine in a larger system where users upload their CV, receive suggested job titles via an LLM, and then browse real job postings — each scored by how well it matches their professional profile.

The Labeling Problem¶

Supervised learning requires labeled data, but no ground-truth dataset exists that maps arbitrary job pairs to alignment scores. Manually labeling 44,100+ examples would be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. This creates a cold-start problem: we need labels to train a model, but generating those labels at scale requires either massive human effort or an alternative strategy.

Solution: LLM-as-a-Labeler (Knowledge Distillation)¶

We solve this using knowledge distillation — a technique where a large, expensive model (the "teacher") generates labels that a smaller, faster model (the "student") learns to replicate. In our case:

  • Teacher: Meta's LLaMA 3 (8B parameters), running locally via Ollama
  • Student: An XGBoost gradient-boosted tree regressor

This approach is also referred to as synthetic labeling or weak supervision in the literature. The LLM possesses implicit knowledge about job relationships, skill overlap, and career path similarity — knowledge that would take thousands of human-hours to encode manually. By querying the LLM systematically, we extract this knowledge into a structured dataset suitable for traditional ML training.

The teacher model evaluates each row by considering:

  • The row's Job Title and Role (what the job actually is)
  • Qualifications required
  • Years of experience
  • Listed skills (first 200 characters)
  • How all of the above relate to the comparator job title

Sampling Strategy¶

The original dataset contains 1,615,942 rows across 147 unique Job Titles. Scoring every row with the LLM would require ~1.6M inference calls — approximately 9 days of continuous local computation. Instead, we employ stratified random sampling:

  • 300 rows per comparator × 147 comparators = 44,100 total labeled examples
  • Each sample is drawn randomly from the full dataset with a fixed seed per comparator for reproducibility
  • At 95% confidence with <2% margin of error, 300 samples per stratum is well above the minimum threshold (~16 rows per stratum required by Cochran's formula)

The sampling was executed in two passes:

  1. Initial pass — 100 rows per comparator (14,700 total). Used to validate the approach, verify score distributions, and establish baseline model performance.
  2. Augmentation pass — 200 additional rows per comparator (29,400 more). Triggered after learning curve analysis confirmed the model was still improving with more data (test MAE dropping from 0.65 at 20% data to 0.55 at 100%, with no plateau).

This incremental approach allowed us to validate quality early without committing to the full computation upfront.

Cost Optimization: Local LLM Inference¶

All LLM inference runs locally using Ollama rather than calling a cloud API:

  • Zero marginal cost — all 44,100 scoring calls executed on consumer hardware (Apple Silicon Mac)
  • Total computation time: ~4.5 hours across both passes
  • Throughput: ~100 rows/minute, limited by model inference speed rather than network latency
  • No data leaves the local machine

For comparison, the same workload on OpenAI's GPT-4 API would cost approximately $50-100 in tokens. The local approach enables unlimited iteration and experimentation at zero incremental cost.

Feature Engineering: Bridging Semantics and Tabular ML¶

The fundamental challenge in training a tabular ML model for this task is that job similarity is a semantic concept. "Software Engineer" and "Java Developer" are highly related, but standard encoding techniques (label encoding, one-hot encoding) represent them as arbitrary unrelated integers. We validated this empirically: models trained with label-encoded job titles achieved only R² = 0.32.

Our solution uses sentence embeddings from the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 transformer model (384 dimensions) to encode:

  • The row's Job Title as a dense vector
  • The Comparator job title as a dense vector
  • The row's Skills text as a dense vector

Additionally, we compute explicit cosine similarity features:

  • Between Job Title and Comparator embeddings (captures title-level alignment)
  • Between Skills and Comparator embeddings (captures skill-level alignment)

These embedding features, combined with the original numeric features (experience, salary, description length, skills count, etc.) and label-encoded categorical features, give the model both semantic understanding and structured signal — yielding a final feature space of 1,179 dimensions.

Script & Data Location¶

  • Label generation script: generate_sample_scores.py (configurable via ROWS_PER_COMPARATOR and OFFSET variables)
  • Generated training data: data/output/samples/ (147 CSV files, one per comparator)
  • Trained model: data/output/models/xgb_job_alignment_model.pkl

The OFFSET parameter controls which random sample to draw — 0 produces the original batch, and values of 1+ generate additional non-overlapping batches that append to existing files. This makes it straightforward to add more training data without regenerating from scratch.

We load all 147 scored CSV files generated by the local LLM labeling pipeline and concatenate them into a single training DataFrame.

numeric_cols = [
    'Experience_min', 'Experience_max', 'Experience_avg', 'Salary', 'Salary_log',
    'latitude', 'longitude', 'Company Size', 'Company_freq', 'Has_Ticker', 'Has_Website',
    'desc_length', 'skills_length', 'resp_length', 'skills_count', 'skills_word_count',
    'job_desc_word_count', 'resp_word_count', 'benefits_count'
]
other_cats = ['Qualifications', 'Work Type', 'Preference', 'Job Portal', 'Company_Sector', 'Role']

emb_model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
print("Encoding...")
jt_embeddings = emb_model.encode(df['Job Title'].tolist(), show_progress_bar=True)
comp_embeddings = emb_model.encode(df['Job_Comparator'].tolist(), show_progress_bar=True)
skills_embeddings = emb_model.encode(df['skills'].fillna('').str[:200].tolist(), show_progress_bar=True)

cosine_sim = np.array([np.dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b)) for a, b in zip(jt_embeddings, comp_embeddings)])
skills_comp_cosine = np.array([np.dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b) + 1e-8) for a, b in zip(skills_embeddings, comp_embeddings)])

df_enc = df.copy()
for col in other_cats:
    le = LabelEncoder()
    df_enc[col] = le.fit_transform(df_enc[col].astype(str))

X = np.hstack([
    df_enc[numeric_cols + other_cats].values,
    jt_embeddings,
    comp_embeddings,
    skills_embeddings,
    cosine_sim.reshape(-1, 1),
    skills_comp_cosine.reshape(-1, 1)
])
y = df['Score'].values
print(f"Features: {X.shape[1]}, Samples: {X.shape[0]}")

def get_score(comparator, job_row):
  # Build features
  numeric_cols = [
      'Experience_min', 'Experience_max', 'Experience_avg', 'Salary', 'Salary_log',
      'latitude', 'longitude', 'Company Size', 'Company_freq', 'Has_Ticker', 'Has_Website',
      'desc_length', 'skills_length', 'resp_length', 'skills_count', 'skills_word_count',
      'job_desc_word_count', 'resp_word_count', 'benefits_count'
  ]
  other_cats = ['Qualifications', 'Work Type', 'Preference', 'Job Portal', 'Company_Sector', 'Role']

  df_enc = df.copy()
  label_encoders = {}
  for col in other_cats:
    le = LabelEncoder()
    df_enc[col] = le.fit_transform(df_enc[col].astype(str))
    label_encoders[col] = le

  # Encode categoricals (use same encoders from training - for demo, just use label encoding)
  cat_values = [label_encoders[col].transform([job_row[col]])[0] if job_row[col] in label_encoders[col].classes_ else 0 for col in other_cats]

  # Embeddings
  jt_emb = emb_model.encode([job_row['Job Title']])
  comp_emb = emb_model.encode([comparator])
  skills_emb = emb_model.encode([job_row['skills'][:200]])

  cosine_sim = np.dot(jt_emb[0], comp_emb[0]) / (norm(jt_emb[0]) * norm(comp_emb[0]))
  skills_cosine = np.dot(skills_emb[0], comp_emb[0]) / (norm(skills_emb[0]) * norm(comp_emb[0]))

  # Assemble feature vector
  numeric_values = [job_row[col] for col in numeric_cols]
  features = np.hstack([
      numeric_values,
      cat_values,
      jt_emb[0],
      comp_emb[0],
      skills_emb[0],
      [cosine_sim],
      [skills_cosine]
  ]).reshape(1, -1)

  # Predict
  score = model.predict(features)[0]
  score = max(0.0, min(5.0, score))

  return score

Conclusion¶

After evaluating four model architectures on the same 44,100-row training set with sentence embedding features, XGBoost consistently outperformed all alternatives:

  • XGBoost: MAE = 0.34, R² = 0.83, 96.2% of predictions within ±1.0
  • LightGBM: MAE = 0.37, R² = 0.81, 95.4% within ±1.0
  • Neural Network (MLP): MAE = 0.41, R² = 0.78, 93.9% within ±1.0
  • Random Forest: MAE = 0.46, R² = 0.72, 92.1% within ±1.0

The selected XGBoost model predicts job alignment scores with an average error of 0.34 points on a 0–5 scale, and 77.5% of its predictions fall within half a point of the LLM-generated ground truth. This level of accuracy is sufficient for ranking job postings by relevance to a user's profile, the primary use case in the application.

The knowledge distillation approach proved effective: a model that runs in milliseconds successfully replicates the judgment of an 8-billion parameter LLM that takes seconds per inference. The entire labeling pipeline ran locally at zero API cost, and the incremental sampling strategy (100 → 300 rows per comparator) demonstrated measurable improvement — confirming that the model benefits from additional data and could be further improved in future iterations by increasing ROWS_PER_COMPARATOR or adding a third offset pass.

The sentence embedding features were the single most impactful engineering decision. Without them (label encoding only), the best model achieved R² = 0.32. With embeddings, R² jumped to 0.83 — a 2.6x improvement in explained variance. This confirms that semantic representation of job titles and skills is essential for this task, and that cosine similarity alone (R² = 0.22) is insufficient without the full embedding vectors as additional features.

Section 4: LLM Integration for CV Optimization and Semantic Job Alignment¶

The objective of this section is to integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) into the recruitment pipeline to enhance CV optimization and semantic understanding of candidate-job alignment.

Unlike the supervised ranking model developed in Section 3, the LLM component is not responsible for generating compatibility rankings or recommendation scores. The ranking and scoring logic remain fully handled by the trained XGBoost regression model and API-based prediction pipeline.

Instead, the LLM layer focuses on:

  • CV enhancement and optimization
  • Semantic restructuring of candidate information
  • Improvement of ATS readability
  • Professional rewriting and keyword optimization
  • Natural language interaction with users

This separation of responsibilities creates a hybrid architecture where:

  • Traditional machine learning handles scalable numeric ranking
  • The LLM handles language understanding and content generation

This design avoids unnecessary LLM inference costs for ranking tasks while preserving deterministic scoring behavior and reproducibility.

AWS Bedrock Deployment¶

To operationalize the NLP layer, we deployed a hosted LLM solution using Amazon Bedrock.

The selected foundation model is:

  • Gemma 3 12B IT

The deployment uses long-term API credentials configured through AWS IAM for authenticated access from the application backend.

Key reasons for selecting Bedrock include:

  • Fully managed infrastructure
  • Scalable inference endpoints
  • Lower operational complexity
  • Secure API-based access
  • Native integration with AWS ecosystem services
  • Elimination of local GPU dependency

Unlike the earlier local LLaMA experimentation used during synthetic label generation, Bedrock enables production-grade deployment with stable inference latency and centralized model management.

The LLM integration is therefore focused on runtime inference for CV enhancement workflows rather than offline synthetic labeling.

Here a shell execution we did to test connectivity to the Bedrock model:

Role of the LLM in the System Architecture¶

The LLM component operates as a semantic enhancement layer within the platform.

Its primary responsibilities include:

  • Rewriting CV sections using professional language
  • Improving ATS keyword coverage
  • Generating optimized summaries
  • Enhancing readability and formatting consistency
  • Aligning candidate descriptions with target job titles
  • Assisting users through conversational interactions

Importantly, the LLM does not perform the final recommendation ranking.

The ranking pipeline remains entirely supervised and deterministic:

  1. Candidate CV data is processed and structured
  2. Feature engineering and embedding generation are applied
  3. The trained XGBoost model predicts the compatibility score
  4. Vacancies are ranked numerically through the ML pipeline
  5. The LLM enhances presentation and textual optimization only

This separation ensures:

  • Faster ranking inference
  • Lower operational cost
  • Higher reproducibility
  • Reduced hallucination risk in scoring
  • Easier evaluation and benchmarking

Bedrock Agent Configuration¶

In addition to direct Bedrock inference calls, we configured an AWS Bedrock Agent using the same Gemma 3 12B IT foundation model.

The agent was initially created using a simple orchestration strategy to validate runtime interaction and response generation.

Current orchestration configuration:

  • Pre-processing: inactive
  • Orchestration: active (default orchestration)
  • Post-processing: inactive

The current implementation uses Bedrock's default orchestration behavior, where the foundation model processes prompts directly through the managed orchestration layer.

At this stage, the orchestration logic remains intentionally simple in order to:

  • Validate end-to-end connectivity
  • Benchmark response quality
  • Test prompt engineering strategies
  • Evaluate latency and runtime behavior
  • Establish the initial production pipeline

Future iterations will extend the orchestration pipeline through:

  • Custom orchestration logic
  • Lambda-based response handling
  • Structured parsing of model outputs
  • Enhanced formatting layers
  • Workflow-specific prompt routing

Planned Multi-Layer Orchestration and Output Improvements¶

Although the current Bedrock Agent configuration uses minimal orchestration, the architecture was intentionally designed to evolve into a three-layer LLM processing pipeline.

The next iteration will introduce a structured multi-stage flow:

1. Pre-processing Layer¶

  • Input normalization (CV text cleaning and structuring)
  • Intent detection (CV optimization vs query handling)
  • Context enrichment (job role, skills extraction)

2. Orchestration Layer¶

  • Prompt routing based on user intent
  • Dynamic selection of generation strategy
  • Temperature-controlled response variation experiments
  • Coordination between CV rewriting, summarization, and keyword optimization tasks

3. Post-processing Layer¶

  • Copy-paste ready CV formatting
  • Structured section generation
  • ATS-friendly output templates
  • Bullet-point normalization
  • Consistent professional tone
  • Improved readability for recruiters

This post-processing stage will likely be implemented through:

  • AWS Lambda integration
  • Structured response parsing
  • Template-based formatting
  • Controlled output validation

A key addition in this phase is systematic experimentation with temperature configurations, allowing the system to balance:

  • Deterministic outputs for ATS-critical sections (low temperature)
  • Creative rewriting for summaries and descriptions (higher temperature)
  • Controlled variability for A/B testing CV optimization strategies

By separating generation into three distinct layers, the system can maintain:

  • Better output consistency
  • Easier maintainability
  • Reduced prompt complexity
  • Fine-grained control over response behavior

Addressing the NLP Feedback¶

Several recommendations from the project feedback were incorporated into the revised architecture.

The updated system now includes:

  • A fully operational NLP pipeline integrated through AWS Bedrock
  • Production-grade LLM inference infrastructure
  • Semantic understanding capabilities through foundation models
  • Hybrid ML + LLM architecture
  • Runtime conversational interaction through Bedrock Agents

However, some recommendations were intentionally not adopted because they do not align with the system's final architecture.

Specifically:

  • The LLM is not responsible for ranking job vacancies
  • Recommendation scores are generated exclusively by the supervised XGBoost model
  • PCA-based dimensionality reduction was not required because the final ranking model already achieved strong performance without meaningful overfitting
  • Clustering validation was not necessary for the production objective, which is ranking quality rather than unsupervised representation learning
  • FAISS similarity retrieval was not adopted because ranking is performed directly through the trained regression model API rather than vector database retrieval

The final architecture therefore prioritizes:

  • Deterministic ranking
  • Low-latency inference
  • Scalable deployment
  • Clear separation between semantic generation and numeric prediction

Hybrid System Architecture¶

The final platform combines supervised machine learning with modern LLM-based NLP services.

Structured ML Layer¶

Responsible for:

  • Feature engineering
  • Compatibility score prediction
  • Vacancy ranking
  • Numeric evaluation
  • Recommendation ordering

Main model:

  • XGBoost Regressor

LLM Layer¶

Responsible for:

  • CV optimization
  • Semantic rewriting
  • ATS enhancement
  • Natural language interaction
  • Candidate assistance

Main infrastructure:

  • AWS Bedrock
  • Gemma 3 12B IT
  • Bedrock Agent orchestration

This hybrid design provides both:

  • High ranking accuracy through supervised learning
  • Flexible language generation through foundation models

while keeping operational costs and complexity under control.

Conclusion¶

This section finalized the NLP integration phase of the project through AWS Bedrock deployment and Bedrock Agent orchestration.

The resulting architecture separates ranking from language generation:

  • The XGBoost model handles compatibility prediction and recommendation scoring
  • The LLM layer focuses on semantic enhancement and CV optimization

This decision preserves the strong quantitative performance achieved in Section 3 while adding modern NLP capabilities suitable for real-world recruitment workflows.

The Bedrock deployment establishes a scalable foundation for future improvements including:

  • Advanced orchestration strategies
  • Structured response pipelines
  • Automated formatting layers
  • Enhanced recruiter-facing outputs
  • Interactive candidate support

The final system therefore combines:

  • Traditional machine learning
  • Semantic NLP capabilities
  • Cloud-based inference infrastructure
  • Hybrid recommendation architecture

into a unified intelligent recruitment platform.

Activity 3 Model Evaluation Answers¶

1. What algorithm can be used as a baseline to predict the target variable? A strong and appropriate baseline for this regression problem is a simple Linear Regression model or alternatively a Random Forest Regressor with default parameters. Linear Regression provides a minimal performance benchmark under a strong assumption of linear relationships between features and the compatibility score, while Random Forest offers a slightly more robust non-linear baseline without extensive tuning. These baselines help quantify the gain obtained from more advanced models such as XGBoost.

2. Can feature importance be determined for the generated model? Yes. Since the final model is based on XGBoost (gradient-boosted decision trees), feature importance can be directly extracted using built-in methods such as gain, weight, or cover. Additionally, more robust interpretability techniques such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) can be used to analyze global and local feature contributions. This is particularly relevant because the model includes both engineered numerical features and high-dimensional embedding vectors, making interpretability useful for validating that semantic similarity features (e.g., embeddings and cosine similarity) contribute meaningfully to predictions.

3. Is the model underfitting or overfitting the training data? Based on the reported results (R² ≈ 0.83 on the test set and low MAE ≈ 0.34), the model does not show clear signs of either severe underfitting or overfitting. The performance gap between training and test is not indicated to be large, suggesting good generalization behavior. However, due to the high feature dimensionality (1,179 features), mild overfitting risk remains possible and should be monitored using cross-validation and learning curves.

4. What is the appropriate metric for this business problem? Since the task is a regression problem predicting a compatibility score (0–5), the most appropriate metrics are:

  • MAE (Mean Absolute Error) as the primary metric, because it is directly interpretable in terms of average prediction deviation in score points.
  • R² (Coefficient of Determination) as a secondary metric to measure explained variance.
  • Additionally, a business-relevant metric such as Hit Rate within ±1.0 score error is useful because ranking systems are more sensitive to relative ordering than exact numeric precision.

5. What should be the minimum acceptable model performance? A minimum viable performance threshold for deployment should be:

  • MAE ≤ 0.5
  • R² ≥ 0.75
  • At least 90% of predictions within ±1.0 error margin

This ensures the model is sufficiently accurate to support reliable job ranking, where small deviations in score do not significantly affect recommendation quality.

NLP Section Note¶

The NLP component of this system is implemented as a separate semantic enhancement layer using AWS Bedrock with the Gemma 3 12B IT foundation model and an associated Bedrock Agent. Its role is strictly limited to natural language processing tasks such as CV rewriting, ATS optimization, keyword enrichment, and improving the clarity and structure of candidate profiles. It does not participate in ranking or scoring job compatibility, which is fully handled by the supervised XGBoost model to ensure deterministic and reproducible predictions. This separation of concerns avoids unnecessary use of LLM inference for numerical tasks, reduces cost, and improves system stability. The current implementation uses default orchestration within the Bedrock Agent, with pre-processing and post-processing layers kept inactive for now, while future work will focus on introducing structured orchestration logic, configurable temperature settings for controlled variability, and a dedicated post-processing layer to produce fully formatted, copy-paste-ready CV outputs.

Section 4: Alternative Model Evaluation and Model Selection¶

Following the feature engineering and synthetic label generation stages, the next phase focuses on evaluating multiple candidate models for the job alignment prediction task.

The objective of this stage is to identify the model that best approximates the compatibility scores generated during the knowledge distillation process while maintaining strong generalization performance, computational efficiency, and practical deployability.

To ensure a fair comparison, all candidate models are evaluated using:

  • The same feature space (engineered features + embeddings)
  • The same train/test split
  • The same evaluation metrics
  • The same target variable (Compatibility Score)

The evaluated models represent different inductive biases and learning paradigms, allowing a broader exploration of the solution space.

4.1 Candidate Model Justification¶

To satisfy the requirement of evaluating at least 6 models with diverse inductive biases, we select the following candidates:

# Model Family Inductive Bias
1 Ridge Regression Linear (regularized) Assumes approximate linear relationship; L2 penalty controls overfitting in high-dimensional spaces
2 K-Nearest Neighbors Instance-based (lazy) Non-parametric; predictions based on local neighborhood similarity
3 Random Forest Tree-based (bagging) Ensemble of decorrelated trees via bootstrap aggregation
4 XGBoost Tree-based (boosting) Sequential error correction via gradient boosting
5 LightGBM Tree-based (leaf-wise boosting) Histogram-based splitting with leaf-wise growth strategy
6 MLP Neural Network Neural (connectionist) Universal approximator; learns non-linear feature interactions through backpropagation

This selection covers 5 distinct learning paradigms: linear, instance-based, bagging, boosting, and neural. The three tree-based models (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM) are included because they represent fundamentally different ensemble strategies despite sharing the decision tree base learner.

In [79]:
import time
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
from lightgbm import LGBMRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

# Prepare scaled version for models that need it (KNN, MLP, Ridge)
X_train_clean = np.nan_to_num(X_train, nan=0.0)
X_test_clean = np.nan_to_num(X_test, nan=0.0)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train_clean)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test_clean)

# Define all 6 candidates
candidates = {
    'Ridge': Ridge(alpha=1.0),
    'KNN': KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=7, n_jobs=-1),
    'RandomForest': RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=12, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'XGBoost': XGBRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=8, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'LightGBM': LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=8, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1),
    'MLP': MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(256, 128, 64), activation='relu', max_iter=300, random_state=42, early_stopping=True, verbose=False),
}

# Models that need scaled input
needs_scaling = {'Ridge', 'KNN', 'MLP'}

# Train all and collect results
results = {}
trained_models = {}

for name, model in candidates.items():
    Xtr = X_train_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_train
    Xte = X_test_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_test

    start = time.time()
    model.fit(Xtr, y_train)
    train_time = time.time() - start

    start = time.time()
    y_pred = model.predict(Xte)
    infer_time = time.time() - start

    results[name] = {
        'MAE': mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred),
        'RMSE': np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred)),
        'R2': r2_score(y_test, y_pred),
        'Hit_1.0': (np.abs(y_test - y_pred) <= 1.0).mean(),
        'Train_time_s': train_time,
        'Infer_time_s': infer_time,
        'y_pred': y_pred,
    }
    trained_models[name] = model
    print(f"{name:12s} | MAE={results[name]['MAE']:.4f} | R²={results[name]['R2']:.4f} | Train={train_time:.1f}s | Infer={infer_time:.3f}s")

4.3 Hyperparameter Tuning (A3)¶

We perform randomized search over a defined hyperparameter space for each candidate model. To keep computation tractable, we use 3-fold cross-validation with 20 random configurations per model. The primary optimization metric is negative MAE

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
from lightgbm import LGBMRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor

# Best params (Ridge and KNN from search, rest from domain knowledge)
tuned_candidates = {
    'Ridge': Ridge(alpha=100.0),
    'KNN': KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3, weights='distance', p=1, n_jobs=-1),
    'RandomForest': RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=16, min_samples_leaf=1, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'XGBoost': XGBRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=8, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'LightGBM': LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_depth=8, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=63, random_state=42, n_jobs=1, verbose=-1),
    'MLP': MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(256, 128, 64), alpha=0.001, learning_rate_init=0.001, max_iter=300, random_state=42, early_stopping=True,
verbose=False),
}

best_models = {}
tuning_results = {}

for name, model in tuned_candidates.items():
    Xtr = X_train_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_train
    Xte = X_test_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_test

    # 3-fold CV on training set (sequential to avoid segfault)
    scores = cross_val_score(model, Xtr, y_train, cv=3, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', n_jobs=1)

'learning_rate', 'num_leaves', 'min_samples_leaf', 'hidden_layer_sizes']},
        'best_cv_mae': cv_mae,
    }
    print(f"{name:12s} | CV MAE={cv_mae:.4f} (+/- {scores.std():.4f})")

4.4 Performance Comparison (A2)¶

We evaluate all tuned models on the frozen test set using three metrics: MAE (primary), RMSE, and R². We also report the hit rate (predictions within ±1.0 of the true score) as a business-relevant threshold. A Pareto frontier plot visualizes the trade-off between prediction quality and computational cost.

4.5 Statistical Significance (A5)¶

Point metrics alone are insufficient for model comparison. We compute bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 resamples) on MAE for each model, and perform paired bootstrap tests between the top candidates to determine whether performance differences are statistically significant or within noise.

In [82]:
from scipy import stats

def bootstrap_mae(y_true, y_pred, n_boot=1000, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    maes = []
    n = len(y_true)
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        idx = rng.randint(0, n, n)
        maes.append(mean_absolute_error(y_true[idx], y_pred[idx]))
    return np.array(maes)

# Bootstrap CIs for all models
print("=" * 60)
print(f"{'Model':12s} | {'MAE':>6s} | {'95% CI Lower':>12s} | {'95% CI Upper':>12s}")
print("-" * 60)

boot_results = {}
for name, model in best_models.items():
    Xte = X_test_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_test
    y_pred = model.predict(Xte)
    boot_maes = bootstrap_mae(y_test, y_pred)
    ci_low, ci_high = np.percentile(boot_maes, [2.5, 97.5])
    boot_results[name] = {'maes': boot_maes, 'ci': (ci_low, ci_high), 'mean': boot_maes.mean()}
    print(f"{name:12s} | {boot_maes.mean():.4f} | {ci_low:.4f}       | {ci_high:.4f}")

# Paired bootstrap test: top 2 models
sorted_models = sorted(boot_results.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]['mean'])
top1_name, top1 = sorted_models[0]
top2_name, top2 = sorted_models[1]

diff = top2['maes'] - top1['maes']
p_value = (diff <= 0).mean()

print(f"\n--- Paired Bootstrap Test ---")
print(f"{top1_name} vs {top2_name}")
print(f"Mean MAE difference: {diff.mean():.4f}")
print(f"P(top2 <= top1): {p_value:.4f}")
if p_value > 0.05:
    print("→ Statistical TIE: CIs overlap, difference not significant at α=0.05")
else:
    print(f"→ {top1_name} is significantly better (p={p_value:.4f})")

4.7 Error Analysis and Subgroup Disaggregation (A6)¶

We analyze prediction errors across the top-2 models (XGBoost and LightGBM) disaggregated by score range and qualifications level to identify subgroups where performance diverges.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Get predictions from top 2
Xte = X_test
y_pred_xgb = best_models['XGBoost'].predict(Xte)
y_pred_lgbm = best_models['LightGBM'].predict(Xte)

# --- Disaggregation by Score Range ---
bins = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5)]
bin_labels = ['0-1', '1-2', '2-3', '3-4', '4-5']

print("=" * 65)
print(f"{'Score Range':>11} | {'XGBoost MAE':>11} | {'LightGBM MAE':>12} | {'Winner':>8} | {'N':>5}")
print("-" * 65)

for (lo, hi), label in zip(bins, bin_labels):
    mask = (y_test >= lo) & (y_test < hi)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        continue
    mae_xgb = mean_absolute_error(y_test[mask], y_pred_xgb[mask])
    mae_lgbm = mean_absolute_error(y_test[mask], y_pred_lgbm[mask])
    winner = "XGBoost" if mae_xgb <= mae_lgbm else "LightGBM"
    print(f"{label:>11} | {mae_xgb:>11.4f} | {mae_lgbm:>12.4f} | {winner:>8} | {mask.sum():>5}")

# --- Disaggregation by Qualifications ---

    [i for i, x in enumerate(np.array_split(np.arange(len(df)), 1)) for i in x])]

# Use df_enc qualifications mapped back

import tempfile, joblib, os, time

# Compute model artifact sizes
model_sizes = {}
for name, model in best_models.items():
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.pkl', delete=False) as f:
        joblib.dump(model, f.name)
        model_sizes[name] = os.path.getsize(f.name) / (1024 * 1024)
        os.unlink(f.name)

# Inference latency (P50/P95)
latencies = {}
for name, model in best_models.items():
    Xte = X_test_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_test
    times = []
    for _ in range(10):
        start = time.time()
        model.predict(Xte[:100])
        times.append(time.time() - start)
    latencies[name] = {'P50': np.percentile(times, 50) * 1000, 'P95': np.percentile(times, 95) * 1000}

# Interpretability profiles

Interpretability and Deployment Assessment¶

  • XGBoost (selected model): Best accuracy (MAE 0.34), native interpretability via gain/weight/cover + SHAP, compact 6 MB artifact, and 1.2ms P50 inference latency. Ideal for real-time API deployment.
  • LightGBM (runner-up): Fastest training (18s), smallest artifact (2.9 MB), slightly higher latency (5.1ms). Nearly identical performance to XGBoost but statistically inferior.
  • MLP: Competitive accuracy (MAE 0.41) with fast inference (0.4ms), but opaque — requires post-hoc SHAP/LIME for explanations, adding complexity.
  • Ridge: Fully interpretable via coefficients, near-zero latency, but insufficient predictive power (R²=0.60). Useful only as a baseline.
  • RandomForest: Interpretable but impractical — 665s training time, 290 MB artifact, 53ms inference. Too heavy for production.
  • KNN: Worst deployment profile — 606ms inference latency (stores entire training set), 318 MB artifact. Unsuitable for real-time use.

Conclusion: XGBoost provides the optimal trade-off across all dimensions — highest accuracy, strong interpretability, fast inference (1.2ms), and compact size (6 MB). LightGBM is a viable alternative if training speed is prioritized (3x faster to train) at the cost of marginal accuracy loss.

Section 5: LLM Configuration Evaluation for CV Optimization (MA1–MA7)¶

This section evaluates 6 different configurations of the AWS Bedrock Agent used for CV optimization. All configurations use the same foundation model (Gemma 3 12B IT) but vary in orchestration layers, temperature settings, and prompt structure.

The evaluation task is: given a user's CV and a target job posting, produce an optimized CV in markdown format that maximizes ATS compatibility, keyword coverage, and professional presentation.

5.2 Configuration 2 — Pre-processing Layer Enabled (temp=0.7)¶

In this configuration, we enable the pre-processing layer which acts as an input classifier. It categorizes user inputs before they reach the orchestration layer:

  • Category A: Malicious or manipulative inputs → blocked
  • Category B: Missing critical information (no CV or no job posting) → asks user for more
  • Category C: Unrelated to CV optimization → rejected
  • Category D: Valid and complete input → proceeds to orchestration
  • Category E: Follow-up answers to agent questions → proceeds

This adds a safety and validation gate that prevents the model from wasting inference on incomplete or harmful inputs.

5.3 Configuration 3 — Post-processing Layer Enabled (temp=0.7)¶

In this configuration, we enable the post-processing layer which enforces a strict markdown CV template on the model's output. The orchestration layer generates the optimized content freely, then the post-processing layer reformats it into a standardized structure with:

  • Consistent section ordering (Summary → Education → Skills → Experience → Certifications → Projects → Awards)
  • Markdown table for skills categorization
  • Standardized heading hierarchy
  • ATS-friendly keyword prioritization

Pre-processing: OFF Post-processing: ON (template enforcement) Temperature: 0.7 (default)

SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 2)

This however, did nothing to fix it. The problem is that with Gemma 3 12B IT, we encountered a persistent parsing failure. The orchestration parser expects the model to wrap its output in <answer></answer> XML tags, but Gemma consistently outputs triple-backtick markdown code fences instead, causing the default parser to fail with:

"Could not parse raw LLM output"

Despite explicit instructions in both the agent instruction and the orchestration template to avoid code blocks and use <answer> tags, Gemma 3 12B does not reliably follow structured output formatting constraints. This is a known limitation of smaller open-weight models when strict output schema compliance is required.

5.3 Configuration 3 — Full Pipeline with Model Change (Gemma 3 12B → Llama 3.1 8B Instruct)¶

Despite explicit instructions in both the agent instruction and a custom orchestration template override forbidding code blocks and requiring <answer> tags, Gemma 3 12B does not reliably follow structured output formatting constraints. This is a known limitation of smaller open-weight models when strict output schema compliance is required.

Resolution: We switched the foundation model to Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, which:

  • Reliably follows XML tag formatting instructions
  • Produces <answer></answer> wrapped output as required by the Bedrock parser
  • Is fully open-weight and self-hostable (satisfying the MA1 requirement for at least one self-hostable configuration)
  • Demonstrates strong instruction-following behavior without hallucinating non-existent tools

Additionally, the orchestration template was simplified to remove tool/function calling references, since the CV optimization task requires no external tool invocations — the model processes the input directly and produces the optimized CV in a single pass.

Configuration:

  • Foundation model: Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
  • Pre-processing: ON (input classifier)
  • Post-processing: ON (markdown CV template enforcement)
  • Orchestration override: ON (no-tool variant with CRITICAL FORMATTING RULES)
  • Temperature: 0.7

5.7 LLM Configuration Comparison and Selection (MA2–MA4)¶

Results Summary¶

Config Model Pre Post Temp Keyword Alignment Format Consistency Hallucinations Overall
1 Gemma 3 12B OFF OFF 0.7 Medium Poor (no markdown) None Baseline
2 Gemma 3 12B ON OFF 0.7 Medium Poor None Pre-processing works but output unstructured
3 Llama 3.1 8B ON ON 0.7 High Good None Strong candidate
4 Llama 3.1 8B ON ON 0.3 High Excellent None Conservative, consistent
5 Llama 3.1 8B ON ON 0.9 Low Inconsistent Yes (invented project) Unreliable
6 Llama 3.1 8B ON ON 0.5 High Excellent None Best overall

Final Selection: Configuration 6 (temp=0.5)¶

Configuration 6 (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, full pipeline, temp=0.5, strict prompt) is selected as the production configuration because it achieves the best balance between:

  • Keyword coverage: Naturally incorporates job posting terminology (Go, Scala, Spark, Kafka, Kubernetes, distributed systems)
  • Format consistency: Reliable markdown structure with proper headings, tables, and bullet points
  • Factual accuracy: Zero hallucinations — all content traceable to the original CV
  • Professional tone: Strong action verbs and quantified metrics without over-embellishment
  • ATS optimization: Skills prioritized by relevance to target role

Temperature 0.5 provides enough creativity to rephrase experience compellingly while remaining deterministic enough to avoid the hallucination issues observed at temp=0.9.

Key Findings¶

  1. Gemma 3 12B is unsuitable for structured agent pipelines due to its inability to follow XML tag formatting requirements (<answer> tags), causing parser failures when orchestration layers are enabled.
  2. Temperature > 0.7 introduces unacceptable hallucination risk for CV optimization — a task where factual accuracy is critical.
  3. Pre-processing layer adds value as a safety gate (input validation) with negligible latency cost (~500ms).
  4. Post-processing layer significantly improves output consistency and template adherence.
  5. Llama 3.1 8B Instruct demonstrates superior instruction-following behavior for structured output tasks compared to Gemma 3 12B, while also satisfying the self-hostable requirement (open-weight model available for local deployment)

5.8 Statistical Significance of LLM Configurations (MA5)¶

Since LLM outputs are non-deterministic (temperature > 0), we ran each configuration 3 times and evaluated consistency:

Config Temp Runs with correct format Hallucinations detected Consistent structure
1 (Gemma, no layers) 0.7 1/3 (parser failures) 0/1 No (backtick issue)
2 (Gemma, pre only) 0.7 1/3 (parser failures) 0/1 No
3 (Llama, full, 0.7) 0.7 3/3 0/3 Yes
4 (Llama, full, 0.3) 0.3 3/3 0/3 Yes
5 (Llama, full, 0.9) 0.9 3/3 1/3 (invented project) No
6 (Llama, full, 0.5) 0.5 3/3 0/3 Yes

Findings:

  • Configs 3, 4, and 6 are statistically tied on format reliability (100% success rate)
  • Config 5 (temp=0.9) introduces variance that produces hallucinations in ~33% of runs
  • Config 6 (temp=0.5) is selected as the best balance: zero hallucinations, consistent formatting, and sufficient creativity for professional rephrasing
  • Gemma 3 12B is statistically unreliable for structured agent pipelines (fails ~67% of the time)

5.9 Error Analysis by Configuration (MA6)¶

Errors are categorized by failure stage:

Error Type Config 1 Config 2 Config 3 Config 4 Config 5 Config 6
Parser failure (model ignores XML tags) Yes Yes No No No No
Generation failure (incomplete CV) No No No No No No
Hallucination (invented content) No No No No Yes No
Format failure (wrong markdown structure) Yes Yes No No Partial No
Information loss (dropped CV sections) No No No No No No

Disaggregation by error stage:

  1. Retrieval stage: Not applicable — no RAG or external retrieval is used. All information comes from the user input.
  2. Generation stage: Config 5 (temp=0.9) is the only configuration that generates factually incorrect content (hallucinated "AWS and IBM Cloud Platforms" as a project).
  3. Format stage: Gemma-based configs (1, 2) consistently fail format requirements due to the model's inability to follow <answer> tag instructions. Llama-based configs resolve this entirely.

Subgroup analysis: The CV optimization task does not have natural subgroups in the same way tabular models do. However, we observe that longer job postings (>1500 tokens) produce better keyword alignment across all configs, while shorter postings result in more generic summaries.

5.10 Cost, Interpretability, and Vendor Lock-in (MA7)¶

Dimension Gemma 3 12B (Configs 1-2) Llama 3.1 8B (Configs 3-6)
Cost per query ~2,500 input + ~900 output tokens ≈ $0.003 ~2,500 input + ~900 output tokens ≈ $0.002
Latency (P50) ~10s ~8s
Self-hostable Yes (open-weight, available via Ollama/vLLM) Yes (open-weight, available via Ollama/vLLM)
Vendor lock-in Low — multi-cloud (Bedrock, Vertex, self-hosted) Low — multi-cloud (Bedrock, Vertex, self-hosted)
Data residency AWS us-west-2 (no data leaves region) AWS us-west-2 (no data leaves region)
Interpretability Opaque (black-box generation) Opaque (black-box generation)
Orchestration transparency Pre/post layers provide stage-level tracing Pre/post layers provide stage-level tracing

Cost analysis for production:

  • At 1,000 CV optimizations/month: ~$2–3/month in inference costs
  • Pre-processing adds ~500ms and ~$0.0005 per request (minimal overhead)
  • Post-processing adds ~2s and ~$0.001 per request

Vendor lock-in assessment:

  • Both models are open-weight and can be self-hosted on any infrastructure
  • The Bedrock Agent orchestration layer is AWS-specific, but the core model can be migrated to any provider
  • Lock-in risk: Low — the system can be ported to self-hosted infrastructure (Ollama + custom orchestration) with moderate engineering effort

Interpretability:

  • LLM outputs are inherently opaque — there is no feature importance or coefficient to inspect
  • However, the three-layer architecture (pre → orchestration → post) provides stage-level observability: each layer's input/output is logged in Bedrock traces, enabling debugging of which stage introduced an error
  • This is the maximum interpretability achievable for generative models without fine-tuning or attention visualization

Section 6: Ensemble Evaluation and Final Model Selection (E5)¶

This section evaluates ensemble strategies for the job compatibility ranking model and formalizes the LLM configuration selection as a generative ensemble evaluation (ENS variant).

The evaluation follows the E5/ENS rubric dimensions, addressing both the traditional ML pipeline (XGBoost-based ranking) and the LLM pipeline (Bedrock Agent-based CV optimization).

E5-A: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Ensemble Strategies¶

Homogeneous Ensemble¶

The XGBoost and Random Forest models evaluated in Section 4 are themselves ensemble methods:

  • XGBoost: Gradient-boosted ensemble of 500 decision trees (sequential error correction)
  • Random Forest: Bagged ensemble of 500 decorrelated trees (bootstrap aggregation)

These represent homogeneous ensemble strategies already present in the candidate pool.

Heterogeneous Ensemble (Stacking)¶

To evaluate whether combining diverse models improves over the best individual, we construct a stacking ensemble using the top-3 models from Section 4 as base learners:

  • Base learner 1: XGBoost (boosting)
  • Base learner 2: LightGBM (leaf-wise boosting)
  • Base learner 3: MLP Neural Network (connectionist)

The meta-learner is a Ridge regression trained on the out-of-fold predictions of the base learners.

In [89]:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
import numpy as np
import time

base_learners = {
    'XGBoost': best_models['XGBoost'],
    'LightGBM': best_models['LightGBM'],
    'MLP': best_models['MLP'],
}

oof_preds = {}
for name, model in base_learners.items():
    Xtr = X_train_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_train
    print(f"Generating OOF predictions for {name}...")
    oof = cross_val_predict(model, Xtr, y_train, cv=3, n_jobs=1)
    oof_preds[name] = oof

# Stack OOF predictions as meta-features
meta_train = np.column_stack([oof_preds[n] for n in base_learners])

# Train meta-learner on stacked OOF predictions
meta_model = Ridge(alpha=1.0)
meta_model.fit(meta_train, y_train)

# Generate test predictions from each base learner
test_preds = {}
for name, model in base_learners.items():
    Xte = X_test_scaled if name in needs_scaling else X_test
    test_preds[name] = model.predict(Xte)

meta_test = np.column_stack([test_preds[n] for n in base_learners])

# Ensemble prediction
start = time.time()
y_pred_ensemble = meta_model.predict(meta_test)
ensemble_infer_time = time.time() - start

# Evaluate ensemble
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

ensemble_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_ensemble)
ensemble_r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_ensemble)
ensemble_hit = (np.abs(y_test - y_pred_ensemble) <= 1.0).mean() * 100

print(f"\n{'='*60}")
print(f"STACKING ENSEMBLE RESULTS")
print(f"{'='*60}")
print(f"Ensemble (XGB+LGBM+MLP→Ridge) | MAE={ensemble_mae:.4f} | R²={ensemble_r2:.4f} | Hit±1.0={ensemble_hit:.1f}%")
print(f"XGBoost alone                  | MAE={results['XGBoost']['MAE']:.4f} | R²={results['XGBoost']['R2']:.4f} | Hit±1.0={(results['XGBoost']['Hit_1.0']*100):.1f}%")
print(f"\nDifference (Ensemble - XGBoost):")

E5-A Conclusion¶

The stacking ensemble (XGBoost + LightGBM + MLP → Ridge meta-learner) does not provide meaningful improvement over standalone XGBoost:

  • The ensemble MAE is within the noise margin of XGBoost's individual performance
  • The meta-learner coefficient distribution shows XGBoost dominates the ensemble weight
  • Additional inference complexity (3 models + meta-learner) is not justified by the marginal gain

Decision: The ensemble does not contribute statistically significant lift. XGBoost is retained as the final production model — this is a valid and documented outcome per the evaluation framework.

The homogeneous ensemble strategies (boosting in XGBoost, bagging in Random Forest) were already evaluated as individual candidates in Section 4. The heterogeneous stacking attempt confirms that combining them does not exceed the best individual.

E5-B: Comparative Table with Explicit Thresholds¶

The following table presents all candidate models including the stacking ensemble, ordered by primary metric (MAE). Two horizontal reference lines are included:

  1. E3-BL5 Threshold (minimum viable performance): MAE ≤ 0.5, R² ≥ 0.75, Hit±1.0 ≥ 90%
  2. Best Individual from E4: XGBoost (MAE = 0.341)

The final model selection is defended against the entire table — not just the top 2. A model with marginally higher accuracy is not selected if a statistically tied alternative costs significantly less.

E5-C: Pareto Frontier Interpretation¶

The Pareto frontier connects models that are non-dominated on the quality-cost trade-off:

  1. Ridge (0.1ms, MAE=0.56): Fastest but worst accuracy — below threshold. Useful only as a baseline reference.
  2. XGBoost (1.2ms, MAE=0.34): Optimal trade-off point — best accuracy with near-real-time latency. On the Pareto frontier.
  3. Stacking Ensemble (~6.7ms, MAE≈0.34): Nearly identical accuracy to XGBoost but 5x slower — dominated by XGBoost and therefore NOT on the frontier.

The final model (XGBoost) sits on the Pareto frontier and satisfies all stakeholder constraints:

  • Latency < 5ms (requirement: real-time API response)
  • MAE well below 0.5 threshold
  • 6MB artifact size (deployable to serverless)

No other candidate provides better accuracy at equal or lower cost, confirming XGBoost as the Pareto-optimal choice.

E5-F: Statistically Significant Lift + Stakeholder Criteria¶

This dimension requires four criteria to be simultaneously satisfied:

(a) Statistically significant lift of the ensemble over the best individual from E4 (paired bootstrap test, ≥1000 resamples).
(b) Compliance with the E3-BL5 threshold with margin.
(c) Compliance with stakeholder criteria: latency, interpretability, data resilience, operating cost.
(d) Justified marginal cost: does the metric lift justify the additional complexity?

# (a) Paired bootstrap test: Ensemble vs XGBoost
def bootstrap_mae(y_true, y_pred, n_boot=1000, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    n = len(y_true)
    return np.array([mean_absolute_error(y_true[idx:=rng.randint(0,n,n)], y_pred[idx]) for _ in range(n_boot)])

boot_xgb = bootstrap_mae(y_test, predictions['XGBoost'])
boot_ens = bootstrap_mae(y_test, y_pred_ensemble)
diff = boot_ens - boot_xgb
p_value = (diff <= 0).mean()

E5-F Final Decision¶

Criterion Result
(a) Significant lift over best individual NO — ensemble MAE is statistically tied with XGBoost
(b) E3-BL5 threshold compliance YES — all thresholds passed with margin

Final Model Selection: XGBoost (standalone)

The ensemble does not provide statistically significant lift over the best individual. Per the evaluation framework, this is a valid and documented outcome: "the ensemble does not contribute — the best individual is used."

XGBoost satisfies all four criteria independently and is selected as the production model for job compatibility scoring.

Section 7: LLM Ensemble Evaluation (ENS Variant)¶

This section formalizes the LLM configuration evaluation from Section 5 under the ENS rubric framework, addressing ensemble strategies, diversity, consistency, and cost for generative AI systems.

ENS-A: Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Ensemble Strategies (LLM)¶

Homogeneous Strategies (same model, varied parameters)¶

Strategy Implementation
Temperature variation Same model (Llama 3.1 8B) at temp=0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9
Self-consistency voting 3 runs per config, majority structure selected
Layer ablation Same model with pre/post-processing ON/OFF

Heterogeneous Strategies (different models)¶

Strategy Implementation
Model switching Gemma 3 12B IT vs Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
Cascading Pre-processing classifies → routes to appropriate model/config
Multi-agent debate Not applicable — CV optimization is a generation task with one correct output per input, not a classification where multiple judges vote

Why Traditional Ensembling Does Not Apply¶

Unlike classification/regression where predictions can be averaged or voted on, CV optimization produces a full document as output. There is no meaningful way to:

  • Average two CVs
  • Majority-vote between paragraphs
  • Blend token probabilities across models

Instead, the "ensemble selection" paradigm applies: evaluate multiple configurations and select the best one for production — which is exactly what Section 5 accomplished. The 6 configurations function as ensemble candidates, and Config 6 was selected as the production winner.

The only applicable ensemble technique for generative tasks is cascading (use a cheaper model first, escalate to expensive model if quality check fails), which our pre-processing layer implements by rejecting invalid inputs before they reach the main model.
